claims.text: Q235 steel's corrosion-related degradation or retention of protection across room- and high-temperature regimes is influenced by formation of a protective oxide layer.
Alloy composition affects the protective oxide layer on Q235 steel.
Processing methods affect the protective oxide layer on Q235 steel.
Formation and stability of the protective oxide layer govern corrosion protection.
An optimal alloy composition and processing method will improve Q235 steel's corrosion resistance relative to unmodified Q235 steel.
An optimal alloy composition and processing method will improve Q235 steel's thermal stability relative to unmodified Q235 steel.
The proposed effects apply during aggressive salt exposure at 700–900 °C.
Unmodified Q235 steel is the reference for evaluating changes in corrosion resistance and thermal stability.
The hypothesis is limited by the ranges of alloy composition and processing methods, although those ranges are not defined.
Corrosion rate, oxide-layer thickness, and microstructure would be measured in a controlled experiment varying alloy composition and processing.
An increased corrosion rate after the unspecified 'optimal' composition and processing modifications would falsify the predicted improvement.
